segments.title: Inconstant's unarmoured iron hull and unusually long afterlife
segments.body: Inconstant had an iron hull but no armour. The Royal Navy still regarded the substantial hull as some protection even without an armour belt. Her mixed sail and steam design belonged to the transition between wooden sailing frigates and later protected cruisers. After front-line service, she became a hulk and training vessel under names including Impregnable II and Defiance. She survived from her 1868 launch until sale in 1955, then was broken up in Belgium in 1956, before large-scale warship preservation had become established.

evidence.note: The unarmoured iron-hulled frigate Inconstant later became a training ship, was sold in 1955, and was broken up in 1956.

segments.summary: Inconstant was an iron-hulled screw frigate without armour that later became a training ship and survived until the 1950s.

segments.title: The Wampanoag threat behind Inconstant's design
segments.body: The Royal Navy planned Inconstant as the first of six fast unarmoured frigates designed by Chief Constructor Edward Reed. The class answered the American Wampanoag design, whose exceptional speed made the wooden frigates appear threatening. Serious flaws in the American ships weakened the case for the British programme. The expense of Inconstant and her sisters also mattered, and construction stopped after three ships.

evidence.note: Edward Reed planned six fast frigates in response to the American Wampanoag class, but flaws in the American ships and the British design's cost ended construction after three.

segments.summary: Edward Reed planned six fast British frigates in response to the American Wampanoag class, but flaws in the American ships and the cost of the British design ended the programme after three.

segments.title: Eleven boilers, a giant propeller, and 16 knots
segments.body: Eleven boilers fed a single two-cylinder trunk engine from John Penn and Sons, driving a 23-foot propeller and producing 7,360 indicated horsepower. The ship was 337 feet 4 inches long between perpendiculars, with a beam of 50 feet 4 inches, a draft of 25 feet 6 inches, and a complement of 600. Her displacement was reported at 5,875 tons, and the machinery gave a claimed top speed of 16 knots. The stated range of 2,780 nautical miles at 10 knots is an aggregate from several sources and appears to describe coal-burning steam endurance. Her full ship rig did not face the same fuel limit.

evidence.note: Inconstant's eleven boilers and two-cylinder trunk engine drove a 23-foot propeller with 7,360 indicated horsepower; the ship measured 337 feet 4 inches between perpendiculars, with a 50-foot-4-inch beam and 25-foot-6-inch draft, and combined a full ship rig with a claimed 16-knot speed and stated 2,780-nautical-mile steaming range.

segments.summary: Inconstant paired eleven boilers and a 23-foot propeller with a full ship rig, giving her 16-knot steam performance and ocean endurance under sail.

segments.title: Inconstant's 9-inch and 7-inch rifled muzzle-loaders
segments.body: Inconstant carried ten 12-ton 9-inch guns and six 7-inch rifled muzzle-loaders. The 7-inch guns fired shells of roughly 112 to 115 pounds, including Palliser armour-piercing, common, and shrapnel ammunition. Preserved 9-inch examples at Simon's Town and Hurst Castle show what this heavy battery looked like. The practical distinction is between advertised maximum range and useful range: roughly 9,000 yards for the 9-inch weapon and 5,000 for the 7-inch.

evidence.note: The gun battery, ammunition, surviving examples, and effective ranges.

segments.summary: Inconstant's 9-inch and 7-inch rifled muzzle-loading guns fired common, shrapnel, and Palliser ammunition, with useful ranges below some advertised maxima.

segments.title: Armour-piercing guns on an unarmoured ship
segments.body: The main-deck 9-inch guns sat in a traditional broadside and were credited with penetrating 11.3 inches of wrought iron. The upper deck carried 7-inch guns, including two bow chasers, with a stated penetration of 7.7 inches. Inconstant could therefore damage armoured opponents, but her own hull carried no armour. A return hit from a comparable weapon posed a much greater danger to her than to an armoured target.

evidence.note: Comparison of the guns' stated wrought-iron penetration with the ship's lack of armour.

segments.summary: The ship's broadside could threaten iron armour, although Inconstant's own hull lacked comparable protection.

segments.title: Channel Squadron service followed by eight years in reserve
segments.body: Laid down at Pembroke in 1866, launched in 1868, and fitted out at Portsmouth, Inconstant commissioned in August 1869 for Channel Squadron service. The posting was prestigious, though the Mediterranean Fleet ranked higher. She later joined Rear Admiral Frederick Seymour's Detached Squadron for visits to Scandinavian ports, then paid off in 1872. Eight of her first twelve years from launch were spent in reserve before recommissioning in 1880. This reduced peacetime operating costs while keeping ships maintained and available for wartime expansion.

evidence.note: Construction, commissioning, early squadron duty, payoff, and the logic of reserve service.

segments.summary: Inconstant's early career took her from Pembroke and Portsmouth to Channel and Detached Squadron service, followed by eight years in reserve.

segments.title: A flagship for Seymour and Victorian gunboat diplomacy
segments.body: Frederick Seymour remembered Inconstant from earlier service and requested her as his Mediterranean Fleet flagship when she returned from reserve in 1880. Requesting the ship for the Royal Navy's most prestigious sea command shows that an experienced admiral considered her genuinely useful. Inconstant later served as the Detached Squadron flagship under Richard Meade and, after Meade became ill in Hong Kong, Francis Sullivan. The squadron left Spithead in October 1880 to circumnavigate the world. Its purpose included showing British firepower at foreign ports to reinforce diplomatic demands, and it returned in 1882.

evidence.note: Seymour's choice and the Detached Squadron's diplomatic purpose and world cruise.

segments.summary: Frederick Seymour's choice of Inconstant as a Mediterranean flagship led into a globe-circling Detached Squadron cruise and the coercive diplomacy behind it.

segments.title: World cruise, shipboard fire, and the Anglo-Egyptian War
segments.body: The 1880-82 circumnavigation carried the future George V from Melbourne to Sydney, where he reportedly saw a supposed phantom ship that may have been an ordinary merchant vessel. Inconstant diverted to Simon's Town for possible service in the First Boer War, but hostilities ended before she arrived. On the return voyage, the crew stopped a serious fire by flooding the after compartments. The squadron then went to Egypt, where Inconstant took part in the Anglo-Egyptian War and the bombardment of Alexandria before landing sailors for operations ashore.

evidence.note: The transcript recounts the voyage, fire response, Egyptian diversion, bombardment context, and landing party.

segments.summary: During the 1880-82 circumnavigation, Inconstant carried the future George V, survived a serious fire, and operated in the Anglo-Egyptian War.

segments.title: From fighting ship to accommodation and training hulk
segments.body: After returning to reserve in 1882, Inconstant became accommodation for overflow from the Devonport barracks in 1897. Taken out of service in 1904, she became a gunnery training ship in 1906 and joined the Impregnable boys' training establishment under variants of that name. In 1922 she transferred to Plymouth's Defiance torpedo school, another change that obscures the old frigate's identity in later records. These roles kept the hull institutionally useful long after she ceased to be a credible front-line cruiser. She was the second-to-last Welsh-built naval vessel afloat when broken up.

evidence.note: Inconstant passed from reserve into accommodation, gunnery training, boys' training, and torpedo training before she was sold in 1955 and broken up in 1956.

segments.summary: Inconstant spent her later life as accommodation at Devonport, a gunnery and boys' training ship, and part of the Defiance torpedo school.

segments.title: A fast sailing frigate with retractable steam machinery
segments.body: Inconstant reportedly reached 13.5 knots under sail and was counted among the fastest warships of her day. Her propeller could be hoisted into the hull and her funnels lowered to cut drag when the full ship rig supplied propulsion. The iron hull carried two three-inch layers of oak beneath copper sheathing, which limited biofouling during long deployments. The layered hull may also have helped make her a good seaboat and steady gun platform.

evidence.note: Inconstant reportedly reached 13.5 knots under sail; her propeller could be hoisted, her funnels lowered, and her iron hull carried oak backing beneath copper sheathing.

segments.summary: A hoistable propeller, lowerable funnels, and copper sheathing helped Inconstant combine fast sailing with long ocean service.

segments.title: Why Inconstant made sense on distant ocean stations
segments.body: Repeated flagship service shows that Inconstant's usefulness extended beyond her paper specifications. Her speed, sailing endurance, and behaviour at sea suited a Detached Squadron expected to range around the world. Distant stations and open oceans gave an unarmoured cruiser room to manoeuvre and reduced the likelihood of meeting protected and armoured ships she could not safely fight. Such deployments used mobility and presence while limiting exposure to opponents that could exploit her lack of protection.

evidence.note: Seymour's confidence in Inconstant and her Detached Squadron deployment reflected the ship's speed and ocean endurance, while distant service reduced her exposure to better-protected cruisers.

segments.summary: The ship's speed and ocean mobility were useful abroad, where she was less likely to meet newer protected or armoured cruisers.

segments.title: Comparing Inconstant, Raleigh, and Shah
segments.body: Inconstant, Raleigh, and Shah came from Pembroke, Chatham, and Portsmouth Royal Dockyards respectively, and each used machinery from a different supplier. Inconstant was laid down in 1866, while Shah and Raleigh followed in 1870 and 1871. Brassey's 1887 figures put their costs excluding armament at roughly £213,000, £193,000, and £235,000 in the same order. Shah also carried a revised battery of two 9-inch, sixteen 7-inch, and eight 5-inch guns.

evidence.note: Inconstant, Raleigh, and Shah differed in builders, machinery suppliers, construction dates, and costs, while Shah also carried a revised armament.

segments.summary: Inconstant, Raleigh, and Shah differed in dockyard, machinery supplier, construction date, cost, and armament despite their close relationship.

segments.title: HMS Shah at the Battle of Pacocha
segments.body: Only about three years after commissioning, Shah was serving as Admiral de Horsey's Pacific Squadron flagship when she and the corvette Amethyst fought the Peruvian turret ship Huáscar at Pacocha. The unarmoured British ships had to stay outside Huáscar's turret guns because a damaging hit could be disastrous. Shah could make about 16 knots under steam, but the smaller Peruvian ship manoeuvred more freely in shallow water. Shah launched the first self-propelled torpedo fired in anger, but it missed. The British force failed to contain Huáscar despite its apparent advantages in speed and firepower.

evidence.note: The Battle of Pacocha, Huáscar's shallow-water advantage, and Shah's missed torpedo.

segments.summary: Shah and Amethyst faced the Peruvian turret ship Huáscar in shallow water at Pacocha, where Shah launched the first self-propelled torpedo fired in anger and missed.

segments.title: Shah in the Anglo-Zulu War and later Bermuda service
segments.body: While returning home in 1879, Shah received news at St Helena of the British defeat at Isandlwana and diverted to carry troops to Durban. She contributed sailors and heavy naval guns to the Anglo-Zulu War, where mobile firing trains brought naval weapons ashore. Back in Britain, the ship paid off into the fourth division of steam reserve before transferring to the North America and West Indies Station. She provided accommodation at the Bermuda dockyard from 1897, became a coal-storage hulk in 1904, and was sold in 1919.

evidence.note: Shah's South African diversion, naval contingent, reserve status, Bermuda accommodation role, and coal hulk conversion.

segments.summary: After carrying troops to Durban and landing a naval contingent for the Anglo-Zulu War, Shah spent later decades in reserve, accommodation, and coal-storage roles.

segments.title: How pieces of Shah survived after the ship
segments.body: Shah's iron masts were considered lighter and more durable than Victory's wooden masts. Fitted to Victory during dry-docking work in 1887, they survived long after Shah's hull was sold. The stern plaque associated with the Persian ruler for whom Shah was named is displayed at the St George's Historical Society Museum in Mitchell House, Bermuda. A monument to the crew stands in Victoria Park, Portsmouth.

evidence.note: Shah's material legacy survives in her iron masts aboard Victory, a stern plaque in Bermuda, and a crew monument in Portsmouth.

segments.summary: Shah's hull disappeared, but iron masts fitted to Victory, a stern plaque in Bermuda, and a Portsmouth crew monument preserve material traces of the ship.

segments.title: The industrial dilemma behind building a minor navy
segments.body: The unanswered exercise places the viewer in charge of a smaller South American state in the 1870s or 1880s, outside Chile, Peru, Bolivia, Argentina, and Brazil. The first decision is whether to create a navy and, if so, what force structure the state can support. Developing domestic construction would require iron, other suppliers, and supporting infrastructure. The prompt asks whether the state's industrial base can build and support the fleet it wants. No answer is given, leaving the tradeoff for the viewer to work through.

evidence.note: The transcript poses an audience exercise about naval force design and industrial development for a minor South American state.

segments.summary: The closing design exercise asks what navy a smaller South American state in the 1870s or 1880s could build and what industry would support it.
